title: Exceptions - Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 5i on Exceptions in C++, taught by Mark Redekopp as part of CS103.
main_text: This unit covers Exceptions in C++. The lecture is part of CS103 and is presented by Mark Redekopp. Topics include error handling strategies, the throw/try/catch mechanism, exception hierarchies, custom exceptions, exception safety, and standard library exception usage.
notes_text: Exceptions provide a structured way to handle errors that separates error-handling code from normal program logic. This unit builds on prior knowledge of classes, inheritance, and function call stacks.

title: Thinking About Errors - Vector Class
summary: Introduces error handling by asking what member functions of vector<T> could cause errors and how to communicate those errors to the user.
main_text: Consider the slightly modified vector<T> class. Now consider error conditions: What member functions could cause an error? How do I communicate the error to the user? The vector class declaration shows: template <typename T> class vector { public: vector(); ~vector(); bool empty() const; int size() const; void push_back(const T& val); void insert(size_t loc, const T& val); void erase(size_t loc); T& at(size_t loc); const T& at(size_t loc) const; ... };. Functions like insert, erase, and at could fail if given invalid indices. push_back could fail if memory allocation fails.
notes_text: This motivational slide starts by asking students to think about what can go wrong. The vector class is familiar, making it a good vehicle for introducing error handling. The at() function is notable because it already uses exceptions in the real C++ standard library.

title: Thinking About Errors - ListInt Class
summary: Extends error handling discussion to a ListInt linked list class, asking which functions could fail and how to report those failures.
main_text: Now consider the ListInt class. Now consider error conditions: What member functions could cause an error? How do I communicate the error to the user? The ListInt class uses a linked list with struct Item { int val; Item* next; }; and class ListInt { public: ListInt(); ~ListInt(); void push_back(int v); void pop_back(); void pop_front(); int front() const; int back() const; int& get(size_t i); const int& get(size_t i) const; private: Item* head_; size_t len_; };. Functions like pop_back, pop_front, front, back could fail on an empty list. get() could fail with an invalid index.
notes_text: The ListInt class presents different error-handling challenges than vector. Functions like front() and back() return values, so using the return value for error codes conflicts with the normal return value. This motivates the need for exceptions.

title: pop_front() Error
summary: What happens when pop_front() is called on an empty list? The return value could be used for error codes, but how does the client know what they mean?
main_text: What if I erase a non-existent location? Calling mylist.pop_front() on an empty list (head_=0x0, len_=0). The implementation: void ListInt::pop_front() { // Empty list check? if(head_ == NULL){ // What should I do? } else { Item* temp = head_; head_ = head_->next; delete temp; } }. In this case (since it is void and the return value is not used), we could use the return value and return an error code. But how does the client know what those codes mean? What if I change those codes? This approach is fragile and requires documentation that may go out of sync.
notes_text: This concrete example shows the dilemma: for void functions, error codes could work but are not self-documenting. For functions that return values (like get()), the return channel is already occupied, making error codes impossible without changing the function signature.

images.description: Diagram of an empty ListInt object with head_=0x0 and len_=0, showing that calling pop_front() on this empty list is an error condition.

title: get() Error
summary: When get() is called with an invalid index, the return value cannot be used for error codes since it is already used for the data. An extra reference parameter is clunky.
main_text: What if I try to get an item at an invalid location? Calling mylist.get(7) on a list with only 3 elements (len_=3). The list contains nodes: 3->9->2->NULL. The implementation: int ListInt::get(size_t i) const { // is i a valid index? if(i >= len_) { // What should I do? } else { Item* temp = head_; while(i != 0) { temp = temp->next; i--; } return temp->val; } }. I can't use the return value, since it's already being used for the data. Could provide another reference parameter, but that's clunky: int get(int loc, int &error);. This motivates the need for a separate error reporting mechanism.
notes_text: This is the key motivating example for exceptions. When a function's return value is already used for data, there is no clean way to signal an error through the return value. Adding an error reference parameter works but is ugly and forces every caller to deal with it.

images.description: Diagram of a ListInt with 3 nodes (3->9->2->NULL) showing that get(7) is an invalid access since the list only has 3 elements.

title: Error Handling Options
summary: Lists traditional error handling approaches: return special values, return bools, set globals, print errors, exit, set flags like cin, or silently handle.
main_text: When something goes wrong in one of your functions, how should you notify the function caller? Return a special value from the function? Return a bool indicating success/failure? Set a global variable? Print out an error message? Print an error and exit the program? Set a failure flag somewhere (like "cin" does)? Handle the problem and just don't tell the caller? Each of these approaches has significant drawbacks, which will be discussed on the next slide.
notes_text: This slide catalogs all the traditional (pre-exception) approaches to error handling. Each has problems: special return values can conflict with valid data, bools lose error details, globals are dangerous in multithreaded code, printing assumes a UI context, exiting is too drastic, flags require active checking, and silent handling hides bugs.

title: Issue with Prior Handling Options
summary: Traditional error handling is passive (caller must check), does not work for constructors, and may not be handled at the right level of the call stack.
main_text: None of those are great options. You should always notify the caller something happened; silence is not an option. All the previous strategies were passive. They require the caller to actively check if something went wrong. What if something goes wrong in a Constructor? You don't EVEN have a return value available. What if the function where the error happens isn't equipped to handle the error? We probably want to notify the caller and let them decide. Maybe a function 2 or 3 levels higher is the one that can solve the issue. These problems motivate exceptions as a superior error handling mechanism.
notes_text: The constructor problem is a particularly strong motivator for exceptions. Since constructors have no return value, there is literally no way to signal failure using any of the traditional approaches. Exceptions solve this cleanly.

title: A Hammer: The assert Statement
summary: The assert statement checks conditions and halts the program if false. Good for development but not ideal for production code.
main_text: The assert statement allows you to make sure certain conditions are true and immediately halt your program if they're not. Good sanity checks for development/testing. Not ideal for the final (released) product. Example: #include <cassert> int divide(int num, int denom) { assert(denom != 0); // if false, exit program return(num/denom); }. Assert is a blunt instrument - it terminates the program with no opportunity for recovery. It is useful during development to catch programming errors early, but in production code you want the program to handle errors gracefully.
notes_text: Assert is a preprocessor macro from C. It can be disabled by defining NDEBUG before including cassert, which is typically done in release builds. This makes assert purely a development tool. For production error handling, exceptions are the proper mechanism.

title: Exceptions - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing C++ exceptions as the proper mechanism for error handling.
main_text: This section introduces C++ exceptions, the language's built-in mechanism for structured error handling using throw, try, and catch statements.
notes_text: Exceptions are one of the most important features of C++ for writing robust, maintainable code. They provide a clean separation between error detection and error handling.

title: C++ Exceptions Benefits [1]
summary: Exceptions allow errors to be returned separately from return values, enable specific error identification, and let any caller on the stack handle the error.
main_text: Allow errors to be returned APART from the typical return value. This solves the get() problem where the return value is already used for data. Allows specific identification of the error - different exception types can represent different error conditions. Allows any of the caller functions on the stack to handle the error: The caller, the caller of the caller, the caller of the caller of the caller, etc. When an exception is thrown, the runtime unwinds the call stack looking for a matching catch block. Each stack frame (f1, caller1, caller2) contains a return link to its caller.
notes_text: The stack unwinding mechanism is what makes exceptions powerful. Unlike return-code-based error handling where each intermediate function must check and forward errors, exceptions automatically propagate up the call stack until a handler is found.

images.description: Call stack diagram showing three stack frames: f1 at top (0xbe8), caller1 in middle (0xbf0), caller2 at bottom (0xbf8), each with return link addresses. The exception propagates from f1 up through the stack.

title: C++ Exception Benefits [2]
summary: Exceptions separate error-handling code from normal processing code, improving readability. They give callers the choice of how to handle errors.
main_text: Sets apart error-handling code vs. nominal processing code to aid readability. Decouple and CLEARLY separate the exception processing logic from the normal control flow of the code. They make for much cleaner code (usually). Give the function caller a choice on how (or if) they want to handle an error. Don't assume you know what the caller wants. Example of traditional approach: int status = doit(); if(status == 0){ // Code A } else if(status < 0){ // Code B } else { // Code C }. Which if..else block is the ERROR HANDLING code and which is the nominal processing code? It's often hard to tell looking at someone else's code! With exceptions, try blocks contain normal code and catch blocks contain error code - making it immediately clear.
notes_text: This readability argument is compelling for larger codebases. In traditional error handling, the error checks are interleaved with normal logic, making code hard to follow. Exceptions move all error handling to catch blocks, keeping the normal code path clean and linear.

title: Step 1: The throw Statement
summary: Use throw to signal an error that a function cannot handle. throw halts the function immediately and can return any type, independent of the function's return type.
main_text: Use the throw statement when code has encountered a problem, but cannot handle that problem itself. throw HALTS the function and returns an "error" value. Like 'return' but special. Immediately ENDS the executing function! If no piece of code deals with it, the program will terminate. Gives the caller the opportunity to catch and handle it. What can you "return" with the throw statement? Anything (int, string, etc.)! But some things are better than others. Doesn't have to match the return type. Example: int main() { int x; cin >> x; cout << divide(5,x) << endl; return 0; } int divide(int num, int denom) { if(denom == 0) throw "Denom is 0"; // normal case return(num/denom); }.
notes_text: The throw statement is fundamentally different from return: it does not follow the normal function return path and does not need to match the function's return type. The thrown value travels up the call stack until caught or until the program terminates.

title: Step 2: try and catch Statements
summary: try blocks surround code that may throw. catch blocks handle exceptions by type, like overloaded functions differentiated by parameter type.
main_text: try & catch are the companions to throw. A try block surrounds 1 or more lines of code that may throw an exception. A catch block lets you handle exceptions if a throw does happen. You can have multiple catch blocks but think of catch like an overloaded function where they must be differentiated based on number and type of parameters. Example: int divide(int num, int denom) { if(denom == 0) throw denom; // normal case return(num/denom); }. In main: try { x = divide(numerator, denominator); cout << "Division result: " << x << endl; } catch(int badValue) { cout << "Can't use denominator: " << badValue << endl; x = 0; } // Use x for more computation. Note: We generally don't throw an integer type. More on what you SHOULD throw soon!
notes_text: The try-catch mechanism is the foundation of structured exception handling. The try block marks the code that might fail, and the catch block handles the failure. If no exception is thrown, the catch block is skipped entirely. If an exception is thrown, execution jumps immediately to the matching catch block.

title: Multiple Errors (throws and catches)
summary: A function can have multiple throw statements of different types. A try block can have multiple catch statements, one per type, to handle different error conditions.
main_text: A function can have multiple throw statements (though it will exit when the first executes) and each can throw a different type. A try block can have multiple catch statements (one per type). Example: void swap(int arr[], int len, int i, int j) { if(i >= len) { throw string("bad index i"); } if(j >= len) { throw -1; } int temp = arr[i]; arr[i] = arr[j]; arr[j] = temp; }. In main: int data[5] = {1,2,3,4,5}; int i, j; cin >> i >> j; try { swap(data, 5, i, j); for(int i=0; i<5; i++) { cout << data[i] << " "; } cout << endl; } catch(string& e) { cout << e << endl; } catch(int e) { cout << "Bad j - " << e << endl; }. Note: We generally don't throw ints and strings. More on what you SHOULD throw soon!
notes_text: Using different types for different error conditions enables the caller to handle each error differently. However, throwing primitive types like int and string is considered bad practice. The proper approach is to throw exception objects from the stdexcept hierarchy.

title: Catch Block Notes
summary: Catch by reference to avoid copies. Catch blocks match sequentially by type. catch(...) is a catch-all default for any exception type.
main_text: Should catch by reference (avoid a copy). Will attempt to match the appropriate catch block in sequential order until it finds a compatible type for what is thrown. More about this when inheritance is used with the thrown exception types. catch(...) is like an 'else' or default clause that will catch any thrown type. Example: try { swap(data, 5, i, j); for(int i=0; i<5; i++) { cout << data[i] << " "; } cout << endl; } catch(string& e) { cout << e << endl; } catch(int e) { cout << "Bad j - " << e << endl; } catch(...) { cout << "Unknown exception" << endl; }. The catch(...) block handles any exception not caught by the preceding typed catch blocks.
notes_text: Catching by reference is important for two reasons: it avoids unnecessary copying of the exception object, and it preserves polymorphic behavior when catching base class types. The catch-all catch(...) should be used sparingly and typically only as a last resort.

title: Catch and The Stack (Unwinding)
summary: When an exception is thrown, the program unwinds the call stack looking for an enclosing try-catch block. If none is found, the program terminates.
main_text: When an exception is thrown, the program will work its way up the stack of function calls until it finds an enclosing try...catch block! If no enclosing try...catch block exists in the call stack, the program will quit! Example: int divide(int num, int denom) { if(denom == 0) throw string("div-by-0"); return(num/denom); } int f1(int x) { return divide(x, x-2); // arbitrary } int main() { int res, a; cin >> a; try { res = f1(a); } catch(string& v) { cout << "Problem!" << endl; } }. The call stack shows: divide throws at the top, f1 does not catch it (Not caught, keep going), and main catches it (caught). The exception skips f1 entirely and is handled in main.
notes_text: Stack unwinding is a key feature of exceptions. The exception propagates through f1 without f1 needing any error-handling code at all. This is a major advantage over return-code-based error handling, where f1 would need to check the return value of divide and forward any error to its own caller.

images.description: Call stack diagram showing three frames: divide at top (throws), f1 in middle (not caught, keeps going), main at bottom (caught). Arrows show the exception unwinding from divide through f1 to main's catch block.

title: Catch and The Stack - Recovery Pattern
summary: catch blocks can be used to actually resolve errors, such as re-prompting the user in a while loop until valid input is provided.
main_text: You can use catch() blocks to actually resolve the problem. The while loop and the cin in the catch statement will cause the program to keep getting new inputs until f1(a) does NOT throw. Example: int divide(int num, int denom) { if(denom == 0) throw denom; return(num/denom); } int f1(int x) { return divide(x, x-2); } int main() { int res, a; cin >> a; while(1){ try { res = f1(a); break; } catch(int& v) { cin >> a; } } // We know we have a good result ... }. The pattern is: loop forever, try the operation, break on success, catch the exception and retry with new input. This ensures the program only proceeds when it has valid data.
notes_text: This retry pattern is extremely common in real applications. The catch block handles the error by getting new input and looping back to try again. The break statement exits the loop only when no exception is thrown, guaranteeing that res contains a valid result.

title: What Should You Throw
summary: Do NOT throw primitive values or strings. DO throw exception objects from <stdexcept> like invalid_argument or runtime_error, or define your own exception classes.
main_text: In general, do NOT throw primitive values (e.g. an int, double, etc.) or a string. throw 123; - The value that is thrown may not always be meaningful and provides little context. throw "Someone passed in a 0 and stuff broke!"; - Easy for humans to read but hard for computer to understand. Do throw an object; some are defined already in <stdexcept> header file: throw std::invalid_argument("Denominator can't be 0!"); throw std::runtime_error("Epic Fail!");. These serve as the basis for building your own exceptions. You can always make your own exception class too! The stdexcept classes provide a what() method that returns the error message string.
notes_text: This is a critical best practice. Exception objects provide structured error information that code can programmatically handle. The stdexcept hierarchy provides common exception types that are well-understood across the C++ ecosystem. Custom exception classes should inherit from these standard types.

title: C++ Exception Hierarchy
summary: All standard exceptions derive from std::exception. Key subclasses include logic_error (preventable bugs) and runtime_error (unpredictable failures).
main_text: Using an inheritance hierarchy is recommended and C++ provides one in <stdexcept>. All exceptions are derived from std::exception. bad_alloc is thrown by new if not enough memory is available. out_of_range is thrown by vector::at if bad index is given. logic_error: errors that the programmer should have been able to avoid. runtime_error: errors that could not be detected until the program runs. The hierarchy: std::exception is the root. Under it: logic_error (with children invalid_argument, out_of_range), runtime_error (with children range_error, overflow_error, underflow_error), bad_cast, and bad_alloc.
notes_text: The distinction between logic_error and runtime_error is important: logic_errors represent bugs in the code (like passing an invalid argument), while runtime_errors represent external conditions (like file not found, network failure). This hierarchy enables catch blocks to handle errors at different levels of specificity.

images.description: Class hierarchy tree diagram. std::exception at the root branches to logic_error, runtime_error, bad_cast, and bad_alloc. logic_error branches to invalid_argument and out_of_range. runtime_error branches to range_error, overflow_error, and underflow_error.

title: C++ Exception Hierarchy - what() and Usage
summary: std::exception defines what() to return a descriptive message. Use the hierarchy with throw range_error("msg") and catch(range_error& e) { e.what(); }.
main_text: std::exception defines a what() function that returns a message that can be given to the constructor of a derived exception and retrieved when caught. The exception base class: class exception { public: exception(); exception(const exception&); exception& operator=(const exception&); virtual ~exception(); virtual const char* what() const; }. Example: #include <iostream> #include <stdexcept> using namespace std; int divide(int num, int denom) { if(denom == 0) throw range_error("Div by 0"); return(num/denom); } int main() { int res, n, d; cin >> n >> d; while(1){ try { res = divide(n,d); cout << "Result is " << res << endl; break; } catch(range_error& e) { cout << e.what() << endl; cin >> n >> d; } } return 0; }.
notes_text: The what() function is virtual, enabling polymorphic access to the error message through base class references. Catching by reference (range_error& e) is essential for this polymorphism to work correctly. The message passed to the constructor is stored and returned by what().

title: You Can/Should Define Your Own Exceptions
summary: Create custom exception types by inheriting from std::exception or its subclasses. Catch blocks match on TYPE, so custom types enable precise error handling.
main_text: You can define your own exceptions. Because catch statements execute based on the TYPE of exception thrown, it is recommended to make your own exception types (structs/classes). It is recommended you inherit from std::exception or one of its subclasses. Example: struct DivByZero : public std::range_error { DivByZero(const char* what) : range_error(what) { } };. Then: int divide(int num, int denom) { if(denom == 0) throw DivByZero("Div by 0"); return(num/denom); }. In main: while(1){ try { res = divide(n,d); break; } catch(DivByZero& e) { cout << e.what() << endl; cin >> n >> d; } } return 0;. The custom DivByZero type inherits what() from range_error and can be caught specifically.
notes_text: Custom exception types are preferred because they enable precise catching - you can catch DivByZero specifically without catching all range_errors. The struct inherits the what() mechanism from range_error, so no additional code is needed for the error message.

title: Catch Block Ordering - Most Derived First
summary: Order catch blocks from most derived type first to base type last. A base catch before derived catches all derived types, preventing specific handling.
main_text: Best practice: Order your catch statements from the MOST derived type first to the base type. Why? Recall: DivByZero is-a range_error. So, a DivByZero can be passed to a range_error catch block. Correct catch ordering: try { doTask(); } catch(DivByZero& e) { // Handle divide by 0 } catch(range_error& e) { // Handle a more generic range_error } catch(exception& e) { // Handle any error derived from std::exception } catch(...) { // Handle any exception not derived from std::exception }. Incorrect catch ordering: try { doTask(); } catch(range_error& e) { // Handle a more generic range_error } catch(DivByZero& e) { // Handle divide by 0 - THIS WILL NEVER EXECUTE! } because DivByZero is caught by the range_error handler first.
notes_text: This is analogous to putting specific if-else conditions before general ones. The compiler may warn about unreachable catch blocks, but it is the programmer's responsibility to order them correctly. The catch-all catch(...) should always be last.

images.description: Exception hierarchy diagram showing std::exception at root with logic_error (invalid_argument, out_of_range) and runtime_error (range_error, overflow_error, underflow_error) branches, illustrating why catch order matters.

title: Re-Throwing Exceptions
summary: Use throw; (with no argument) inside a catch block to re-throw the caught exception to a higher-level handler after performing intermediate actions.
main_text: You may want to catch an exception to take some intermediate action, but you can't fully process the error and so you can re-throw it. May want to log some error in the intermediate function but then throw it again to be handled by the higher level software. Example: int divide(int num, int denom) { if(denom == 0) throw invalid_argument("Div by 0"); return(num/denom); } int f1(int x) { int y; try { y = divide(x, x-2); } catch(invalid_argument& e){ cout << "Caught first here!" << endl; throw; // throws 'e' again } }. In main: while(1){ try { res = f1(a); break; } catch(invalid_argument& e) { cout << "Caught again" << endl; cin >> a; } }. The throw; statement (no argument) re-throws the current exception.
notes_text: Re-throwing is useful in layered architectures where intermediate functions need to perform cleanup or logging but cannot fully resolve the error. Using throw; without an argument preserves the original exception type and any associated data.

title: NEVER Throw from a Destructor
summary: Throwing from a destructor causes undefined behavior because data member and base class destructors may not run, leading to resource leaks and crashes.
main_text: Do not use throw from a destructor. Your code will go into an inconsistent (and unpleasant) state. Or just crash. Because data member or base class destructors may not have the chance to run. Example: class Base { public: Base() { bptr_ = new int; *bptr_ = 0; } virtual ~Base() { delete bptr_; } private: int* bptr_; }; class Composite : public Base { public: Composite() { sptr_ = new string("hi"); inUse_ = true; } ~Composite() { if(inUse_ == true) { throw std::logic_error("Should not be in use anymore"); } // If we throw, do we ever do this code? delete sptr_; } private: string* sptr_; bool inUse_; };. If the destructor throws, delete sptr_ never executes (memory leak), and Base::~Base() may also not run (another leak).
notes_text: This is a hard rule in C++. If a destructor throws during stack unwinding (which happens when another exception is already being processed), the program will call std::terminate(). Even outside stack unwinding, throwing from a destructor prevents proper cleanup of the object's own resources.

title: A Look Ahead: Exception Safety
summary: Be careful not to leak resources when throwing. If dynamic memory is allocated before a throw, it may never be deallocated, causing memory leaks.
main_text: Be careful WHEN you throw an exception that you don't leave the code in a bad state or leak resources. Recall your image or maze project. What's wrong with the code to the right where I throw if the argument is null or I can't open the file? Example: void save(char* filename) { // performs dynamic allocation uint8_t*** image = allocateNewImage(); if(filename == NULL) { throw invalid_argument("null ptr"); // Do we still have an issue? } ofstream ofile(filename); if(ofile.fail()) { throw runtime_error("can't open file"); // Do we still have an issue? } //normal processing // deallocate the image array }. The problem: if either throw executes, the dynamically allocated image is never deallocated, causing a memory leak. The deallocation code at the bottom is skipped.
notes_text: Exception safety is a critical concern in C++ because the language does not have garbage collection. Any throw statement that occurs after resource acquisition but before resource release creates a potential leak. This motivates RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) patterns.

title: A Look Ahead: Using the Stack To Help (RAII)
summary: Stack-allocated objects have their destructors called during stack unwinding. Use RAII wrapper objects to ensure cleanup even when exceptions are thrown.
main_text: Recall: Objects declared on the stack AUTOMATICALLY have their destructors called when the function ends (whether by a normal return or BY A THROW). Read more: C++11 shared_ptr, unique_ptr, etc. Solution: create an ImageDeleter wrapper object on the stack that deallocates the image in its destructor: struct ImageDeleter { uint8_t*** img_; int h_, w_; ImageDeleter(uint8_t*** img, int h, int w) : img_(img), h_(h), w_(w) {} ~ImageDeleter() { for(int i=0; i<h_; i++) { for(int j=0; j<w_; j++) { delete[] img_[i][j]; } delete[] img_[i]; } delete[] img_; } };. Usage: void save(char* filename) { uint8_t*** image = allocateNewImage(); ImageDeleter d(image, h_, w_); if(filename == NULL) { throw invalid_argument("null ptr"); // ImageDeleter destructor will clean up! } // No need for manual deallocation code }.
notes_text: This is the RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) pattern, one of the most important idioms in C++. By wrapping resources in stack-allocated objects, cleanup is guaranteed even when exceptions are thrown. Modern C++ provides smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr) that implement this pattern for dynamic memory.

title: Std Library Exception Usage - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing how the C++ standard library uses exceptions, particularly with cin and file streams.
main_text: This section covers how the C++ standard library uses exceptions. Topics include configuring cin and file streams to throw exceptions on errors instead of using the traditional fail() checking approach.
notes_text: The standard library can be configured to use exceptions for I/O errors, providing an alternative to the manual fail() checking approach covered earlier. This connects the exceptions topic back to the file I/O material from Units 5g and 5h.

title: cin Error Handling (Old Way)
summary: Traditional cin error handling uses if(cin.fail()) with clear() and ignore() to detect and recover from input errors without exceptions.
main_text: The old (traditional) approach to handling cin errors: #include <iostream> using namespace std; int main() { int number = 0; cout << "Enter a number: "; cin >> number; if(cin.fail()) { cerr << "That was not a number." << endl; cin.clear(); cin.ignore(1000, '\n'); } }. This approach uses cin.fail() to detect the error, cerr to print the error message (to standard error, not standard output), cin.clear() to reset the fail bit, and cin.ignore(1000, '\n') to discard the bad input up to the next newline. This is the passive approach discussed earlier where the caller must actively check for errors.
notes_text: This is the approach covered in Unit 5h. While it works, it requires the programmer to remember to check for errors after every cin operation. The exception-based approach shown on the next slide automates this checking.

title: cin Error Handling (New Way with Exceptions)
summary: Call cin.exceptions(ios::failbit) to make cin throw ios::failure exceptions on errors, enabling try-catch-based error handling instead of manual fail() checks.
main_text: The new (exception-based) approach: #include <iostream> using namespace std; int main() { cin.exceptions(ios::failbit); // tell "cin" it should throw int number = 0; try { cout << "Enter a number: "; cin >> number; // cin may throw if can't get an int } catch(ios::failure& ex) { cerr << "That was not a number." << endl; cin.clear(); // clear out the buffer until a '\n' cin.ignore(std::numeric_limits<int>::max(), '\n'); } }. The key difference is cin.exceptions(ios::failbit) which configures cin to automatically throw an ios::failure exception whenever the fail bit would be set. This converts passive checking into active exception throwing. The catch block still needs to call clear() and ignore() to reset the stream state.
notes_text: This approach is cleaner because the error is automatically signaled via exception rather than requiring the programmer to check fail() after every operation. The ios::failure exception type is part of the standard library. std::numeric_limits<int>::max() provides a large number to clear the entire input buffer.

title: Other Exceptions Notes
summary: Think about WHERE to handle errors: handle locally if you can, otherwise let the caller handle it. ifstream can also be configured to throw with exceptions().
main_text: Think about where you want to handle the error. If you can handle it, handle it. If you can't, then let the caller. Example: #include <iostream> #include <stdexcept> using namespace std; int f1(char* filename) { ifstream ifile; ifile.exceptions(ios::failbit); // will throw if opening fails ifile.open(filename); // Should you catch exception here // Or should you catch it in main() } int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { readFile(argv[1]); ... }. The question is where to put the try-catch: in f1() where the error occurs, or in main() which might be better equipped to handle it (e.g., by prompting the user for a different filename). The answer depends on which function has the context to resolve the error.
notes_text: This slide emphasizes a key design decision in exception handling: the function that detects the error is not always the best function to handle it. By letting exceptions propagate, you allow the error to be handled at the most appropriate level of the call stack. The exceptions() method works on any stream, including ifstream.
